Corven Spark Program — Week 1 Progress Report
Project: Corven: A Browser-Based IDE for Building on CKB and Fiber Network
Reporting Period: 12–16 October 2026
Status: Week 1 activities underway
Project Website: https://corvanide.space/
GitHub: GitHub - corvenide/corven-fronted: Corven – Cloud Development Infrastructure for CKB · GitHub
1. Overview
During Week 1, I conducted a live Google Meet session to demonstrate the Corven IDE platform to participants associated with the Kisumu developer outreach event. The session lasted approximately one hour and focused on introducing the platform, demonstrating its existing capabilities, and gathering initial feedback on areas that need improvement.
The demonstration provided an opportunity to show how Corven aims to simplify CKB development by bringing the development environment, workspace tools, and blockchain development workflow into the browser.
The feedback received highlighted several improvements that could make the platform more accessible to new developers, improve wallet connectivity, and support community contributions.
A Google Form will also be provided to participants to record attendance and collect structured feedback. The responses will support the project’s user-testing documentation and subsequent progress reports.
2. Activities Completed
Live platform demonstration
A one-hour Google Meet session was conducted as part of the Kisumu outreach activities.
The session introduced Corven IDE, demonstrated the platform, and provided an opportunity for participants to share their experiences, identify usability issues, and suggest additional features.
The demonstration was an initial engagement activity rather than a completed three-hour hands-on testing session. Further structured testing and feedback collection will be conducted as the project progresses.
Initial feedback collection
The demonstration generated six main areas of feedback:
Social login support for wallet connectivity.
External wallet connectivity in the installed web app.
Functionality of the built-in browser tool.
A guided first-time user tutorial.
In-platform video tutorials.
Open-source access and community contributions.
These observations will help inform the project’s development priorities and the design of subsequent hands-on testing sessions.
3. Feedback Received and Planned Responses
3.1 Social login through Corven Connect
Feedback: Participants recommended adding social login options to simplify the wallet connection and onboarding experience.
Planned response: Investigate integration of Corven Connect, a wallet-connectivity tool currently being developed by Corven on top of the CCC wallet-connect infrastructure. The intended direction is to support a more accessible onboarding experience, including social login where supported by the integration.
Status: Feedback received; integration and implementation remain pending.
3.2 External wallet connectivity in the installed web app
Feedback: The installed version of the web app does not connect successfully with external wallets such as MetaMask.
Planned response: Investigate wallet-provider detection, browser compatibility, and connection handling in the installed application. The implementation will need to distinguish between supported wallet providers and browser or installation limitations.
Status: Issue identified; investigation and testing required.
3.3 Built-in browser tool
Feedback: The browser tool within Corven IDE does not work as expected.
Planned response: Investigate the browser preview workflow, workspace connectivity, and any related routing or runtime issues. The goal is to ensure developers can preview and interact with applications running inside their workspaces.
Status: Issue identified; debugging and validation required.
3.4 First-time user tutorial
Feedback: New users would benefit from a guided introduction explaining how to use the platform.
Planned response: Develop an onboarding tutorial covering the essential workflow, from opening a workspace to using the terminal, working with contract templates, building and testing contracts, and deploying to the available development environment.
Status: Planned improvement.
3.5 Video guides within Corven IDE
Feedback: Participants recommended adding video tutorials directly within the platform.
Planned response: Prepare short instructional videos demonstrating important workflows, including workspace creation, contract development, debugging, deployment, and relevant Fiber Network features as they become available.
Status: Planned improvement.
3.6 Open-source contributions
Feedback: Participants recommended making the project openly available to encourage community participation and contributions.
Planned response: Prepare the relevant repository, documentation, licensing, and contribution guidelines so developers can inspect the codebase, report issues, and contribute improvements. The publication process will also clarify which components and configurations are ready for public contribution.
Status: Planned improvement; repository and contribution readiness will be verified before the public release is announced.
4. Attendance and Structured Feedback Collection
A Google Form will be shared with participants to document attendance and gather structured feedback following the demonstration and subsequent testing sessions.
The form will capture relevant information such as:
Participant name or preferred handle.
Developer club or institution, where applicable.
Previous experience with CKB and blockchain development.
General feedback on the Corven IDE demonstration.
Usability issues encountered.
Suggested features and improvements.
Interest in participating in future testing sessions.
For reporting purposes, the form responses will be used to distinguish participants who attended the initial online demonstration from those who participate in future hands-on sessions.
The collected information will support attendance records, feedback analysis, and the final user-testing report. Any public release of survey data will be anonymized, and identifiable information or participant quotations will only be published where appropriate consent has been obtained.
Google Form: [Link to be added once the form is available]
5. Progress Against Project Deliverables
Deliverable
Week 1 progress
1. Fiber playground
Existing Fiber development work remains in progress; integration and verification are pending.
2. Fiber starter templates
Planned for development and validation in the upcoming weeks.
3. Getting-started guide
Initial user feedback has identified the need for clearer onboarding documentation.
4. Open-source repository
Public contribution readiness and documentation are to be addressed.
5. Stable public deployment
Deployment stability and the planned concurrent-workspace load test require verification.
6. Three hands-on testing sessions
Initial one-hour online demonstration conducted; this is not counted as a completed full hands-on testing session.
7. User-testing report
Initial qualitative feedback documented; structured attendance and survey collection is planned.
8. Demo video
Planned for a later project stage.
9. Final completion report
To be prepared at the end of the project, including deliverable verification and funding expenditure.
6. Priorities for Week 2
Based on the initial feedback and the project’s original timeline, the following activities will be prioritized:
Investigate and address the built-in browser preview issue.
Investigate external wallet connectivity in the installed web app.
Assess the integration requirements for Corven Connect and social login.
Begin implementing the first-time onboarding tutorial and plan the in-platform video guides.
Prepare the repository and documentation for community contributions.
Share the Google Form for attendance and structured feedback collection.
Continue developing and integrating the Fiber playground and starter templates.
Conduct further developer engagement and collect feedback to guide subsequent iterations.
Priorities may be adjusted according to the severity of identified issues and progress on the core Fiber deliverables.
7. Conclusion
Week 1 established an initial feedback loop between Corven and the developer community through a live Google Meet demonstration connected to the Kisumu outreach activity.
The feedback highlighted opportunities to improve onboarding, wallet connectivity, application previews, instructional resources, and open-source participation. These observations will inform the next development and testing activities.
The project will continue to document progress against the published deliverables and collect attendance and feedback evidence through a Google Form and subsequent hands-on sessions. The distinction between initial demonstrations and completed structured testing sessions will be maintained in project reporting.
Further updates will document implementation progress, testing outcomes, and any changes to the project timeline.
Submitted by: Jimleston Osoi

topics.title: QuotaCell: Let your team spend without handing over the treasury

recent_posts.topic_title: QuotaCell: Let your team spend without handing over the treasury
recent_posts.author: Ticoworld
recent_posts.content_text:
Imagine you’re running a project with a small team.
There are expenses to handle, suppliers to pay, and people who need to get things done.
You can’t be available to approve every single payment. But you also don’t want to give everyone unrestricted access to the treasury.
So how do you let people spend independently while keeping control of the funds?
That’s the problem I’ve been working on with QuotaCell.
Here’s how it works
Say your project treasury holds 200 tokens.
You want Alice and Ben to handle payments, but you’ve only approved 100 tokens for them to spend altogether.
Alice has a personal limit of 70 tokens, and Ben has a limit of 50. Each can only pay their approved recipient.
The important thing is that they’re both spending from the same 100-token allowance.
If Alice spends 60, Ben can spend another 40, not 50.
Once that 100 is exhausted, neither of them can make another payment under that allowance, even though the treasury still has funds.
Adding more tokens to the treasury doesn’t reset it. Neither does receiving a payment back. The owner has to explicitly renew the spending authority.
And Alice and Ben can make their permitted payments without needing the owner to approve every transaction.
Why CKB?
What interested me wasn’t just displaying a budget or tracking how much each person had spent.
It was making those restrictions enforceable even when someone isn’t using our application.
With QuotaCell, the shared allowance is part of a native CKB policy protecting the funds.
That means someone can have a valid signing key, construct a transaction using another tool, and still have that transaction rejected if it breaks the spending rules.
The limits don’t depend on QuotaCell’s server agreeing to enforce them.
The owner also retains authority to revoke permissions and recover the protected funds through the policy’s supported recovery rules.
I think that’s an interesting foundation for building applications where people need freedom to act, but not unlimited authority.
There’s more we can build around this
Team spending is where QuotaCell started, but we’ve also been investigating how the same approach could support other applications.
Autonomous agents are one particularly interesting direction.
Imagine two agents handling different operational tasks. One pays an approved data provider, while another pays for a separate service. They have their own keys and restrictions, but share one overall spending allowance.
We’ve already investigated this architecture against existing CKB agent and wallet infrastructure. The current policy can accommodate two software-controlled signers without changing its core spending rules. The next step is connecting those agents through independent transaction builders and testing the complete flow.
There are other possibilities too.
A project could give several contributors controlled spending authority from a sponsored budget. A team could manage delegated operational expenses without issuing unrestricted treasury keys.
We’ve also examined shared access to AI services and other limited resources, including how existing gateways and access-receipt infrastructure could help. That needs a different enforcement approach because spending tokens and consuming an off-chain service aren’t the same thing.
What connects these applications is the idea of sharing limited authority without surrendering control of the entire resource.
What we’ve built
QuotaCell already has a compiled native CKB spending policy that we’ve tested through local CKB verification.
We’ve run 89 verification cases, with all 89 producing their expected results: 33 accepted transactions and 56 rejected transactions.
The cases cover permitted payments, shared allowance exhaustion, attempts to bypass restrictions, invalid policy changes, owner administration, and recovery behavior.
The current implementation supports a specific synthetic xUDT profile with two delegates and fixed recipient rules. It’s not yet deployed to a public network or independently audited.
We’re now moving from that native foundation toward the transaction-building, signing, recovery, and application experience needed to make QuotaCell practical. Supporting the assets and payment workflows teams actually use is an important part of that work.
Where we’re going
I want QuotaCell to become something a project owner can actually use to manage delegated spending, while making the underlying policy useful to other CKB applications too.
We’ve already learned quite a bit from examining existing wallets, agent infrastructure, native CKB scripts, and access-control systems. There’s useful work to build on, and there are also areas where new infrastructure could make a difference.
I’m sharing QuotaCell here because I think the underlying idea has room to grow beyond the original team-spending use case.
If you’re building wallets, working with agents, managing project funds, or experimenting with shared resources on CKB, I’d love to hear the situations where this kind of control could be useful, along with approaches or limitations we should consider.
I’ll keep sharing meaningful progress as QuotaCell develops, and I hope some of the ideas and technical discussions here can help shape what we build next.

topics.title: CellRoute / FiberPay — CKB development tools with live asset inspection

recent_posts.topic_title: CellRoute / FiberPay — CKB development tools with live asset inspection
recent_posts.author: Dat_Nguyen_Tu
recent_posts.content_text:
Hi Nervos community,
I am building CellRoute / FiberPay, a CKB application that brings development labs and payment experiments into one portal. I would like to share the current progress and get feedback from developers in the ecosystem.
Live app: https://cellroute.vercel.app/
Source: GitHub - ntudatit/cell-route · GitHub
What the project includes
Simple Lock: deployment manifest checks, lock-address derivation, live capacity lookup, and funding/unlocking transaction preparation.
Token Lab: sUDT/xUDT transaction workflows with wallet review and live-input checks.
Spore/DOB: asset reading and transaction review, with a bounded local DOB/0 reference preview.
SSRI Inspector: configurable service/script inputs, code identity checks, method queries and public receipt export.
RGB++ Inspector: read-only Bitcoin UTXO / CKB Cell binding inspection on paired Mainnet or Testnet networks.
Fiber experiments: two-node invoice/payment workflows requiring configured relays and funded channels.
Runtime tools and per-feature developer consoles for inspecting results and errors.
These capabilities have different prerequisites and verification levels. A UI workflow being implemented does not mean its funded on-chain lifecycle has been verified.
Latest progress: RGB++
The Week 10 work adds live lookup from a user-supplied CKB OutPoint or Bitcoin txid/vout. The inspector checks network genesis and deployment identity, decodes the binding, reports each chain’s state separately and exports public receipts. An advanced regression tool reproduces an upstream fixture’s virtual transaction commitment and deliberate mismatch cases.
Public queries captured on 15 October 2026 identified a live Mainnet CKB Cell bound to an unspent Bitcoin UTXO. The client also checked Bitcoin transaction Merkle inclusion against the API-supplied block header.
This is not full RGB++ SPV verification: the header chain was not independently validated and the RGB++ lock was not executed by this inspector. No RGB++ transfer was signed or broadcast. Results are never labeled cross-chain complete.
Validation and limits
The latest local validation passed 121 portal unit tests across 21 files, 9 Labs browser tests, 4 runtime parser tests, and the production build. These totals cover the broader project, not RGB++ alone. Browser tests include recorded-response replay; actual public-network observations are recorded separately.
The production build still reports a large-bundle warning. Some workflows require operator deployments, compatible services, interactive wallets and funds. The deployed website may differ from the latest local source until the changes are deployed. I am sharing this as a work in progress, not an audited production payment service.
Week 10 report and evidence links:
github.com/ntudatit/cell-route

# Week 10 — RGB++ and Bitcoin UTXO / CKB Cell Binding
**Project:** CellRoute / FiberPay
**Report date:** 16 October 2026
**Network observations:** 15 October 2026
**Status:** Read-only inspection and mismatch tests implemented and reproduced. Full RGB++ proof verification and signed transfer remain incomplete.
## Objective
Understand how an RGB++ asset Cell on CKB is bound to a Bitcoin UTXO, how transaction commitments connect the two chains, and which evidence is required before claiming protocol validation or completion.
In my understanding, the Bitcoin UTXO acts as a single-use seal. The CKB Cell carries asset data and a lock that references that seal. Decoding this reference establishes a data relationship; it does not prove authorization, Bitcoin consensus, or successful RGB++ contract execution. A transaction commitment binds selected transaction data, while a compatible proof and contract validation establish additional conditions that a simple lookup cannot establish.
## Implemented in CellRoute
The `/rgbpp` page now opens a live, read-only inspector. Users can select Bitcoin Mainnet / CKB Mainnet or Bitcoin Testnet3 / CKB Testnet and provide their own CKB OutPoint or Bitcoin txid/vout. No bundled example is required to start a lookup.
The client checks network genesis and deployment identity, decodes RGB++ lock args, observes UTXO spend state and Cell live status, and exports a receipt with public responses and observation times. UTXO searches support paginated CKB indexer results and node rechecks. Empty indexer results do not prove that an asset never existed.
The original public fixture remains available under advanced regression tools. It reproduces the virtual transaction commitment and supports deliberate mismatch checks without broadcasting invalid transactions. Arbitrary live commitment reconstruction is not claimed by the live lookup.
This file has been truncated. show original
Feedback welcome
I would appreciate feedback on the inspector’s evidence boundaries, compatible RGB++ proof-verification infrastructure, and which developer workflow would be most useful to improve next.
My next steps are investigating compatible SPV/client-state verification, preparing a separately reviewed test-network transfer, and continuing with xUDT extensions.

Decoding this reference establishes a data relationship; it does not prove authorization, Bitcoin consensus, or successful RGB++ contract execution. A transaction commitment binds selected transaction data, while a compatible proof and contract validation establish additional conditions that a simple lookup cannot establish.

## Implemented in CellRoute

The `/rgbpp` page now opens a live, read-only inspector. Users can select Bitcoin Mainnet / CKB Mainnet or Bitcoin Testnet3 / CKB Testnet and provide their own CKB OutPoint or Bitcoin txid/vout. No bundled example is required to start a lookup.

The client checks network genesis and deployment identity, decodes RGB++ lock args, observes UTXO spend state and Cell live status, and exports a receipt with public responses and observation times. UTXO searches support paginated CKB indexer results and node rechecks. Empty indexer results do not prove that an asset never existed.

The original public fixture remains available under advanced regression tools. It reproduces the virtual transaction commitment and supports deliberate mismatch checks without broadcasting invalid transactions. Arbitrary live commitment reconstruction is not claimed by the live lookup.

Feedback welcome

I would appreciate feedback on the inspector’s evidence boundaries, compatible RGB++ proof-verification infrastructure, and which developer workflow would be most useful to improve next.

My next steps are investigating compatible SPV/client-state verification, preparing a separately reviewed test-network transfer, and continuing with xUDT extensions.

recent_posts.topic_title: [DIS] RIVET: Decentralized GitHub Backup, Timestamping and Restore on CKB
recent_posts.author: psawyerberlin
recent_posts.content_text:
Nice work getting a working demo on testnet. Backup with a restore path is a real gap, and splitting restore into Exact and Attribution modes is the right call. Two technical points:
1. Anchoring for the deletion case. If GitHub deletes the repo, the anchor is the only independent reference left. What matters then is: does the restored copy match what was backed up? Anchoring a hash of the sorted refs and their tip commits answers that directly. After restore, anyone can recompute it from the bundle with plain git and compare it to the cell, with no GitHub and no Rivet server involved. Most repos are still SHA-1, so I’d also anchor a SHA-256 of the bundle itself. That lets the copy retrieved from IPFS or Arweave be checked byte for byte before restoring.
2. Cell lifecycle and cost per push. With auto-sync on every push, do you consume the previous anchor cell into the new one, or create a fresh cell each time? Consuming and replacing keeps locked capacity flat, and the transaction chain becomes the version history for free. Creating new cells makes the subsidy grow with activity. This is the model I use in VeriCell.net (disclosure: I build it). Each new version consumes the previous live cell, so the live cell always shows the current state and older versions stay verifiable as consumed cells. Happy to compare notes if a shared manifest or verification format makes sense.
Good luck with the vote.

recent_posts.author: Jedi_dtechmaker
recent_posts.content_text:
Thanks for the feedback and the vote!
To answer your questions.
Anchoring & deletion case: Great point. Right now we Merkle-tree all commit hashes (git log --all), but you’re spot on about refs and tip commits. Adding the sorted refs hash + a SHA-256 of the bundle itself makes offline CLI verification (git show-ref / sha256sum) trivial without touching our servers. We’re adding both to the anchor payload.
Cell lifecycle: We already consume and replace! Each backup takes the previous anchor cell as an input and outputs the updated one. Capacity stays locked flat at ~93 CKB per repo, and the transaction chain gives us the immutable version history for free.
And i am definitely down to compare notes!!!
